prompt: In many countries, a high proportion of young people who are released from prison commit further offences within a short period. What are the reasons for this, and how could the situation be improved?
essay:
A striking proportion of young people released from custody are back before the courts within a year, which suggests that whatever the sentence was intended to achieve, it is not being achieved. The reasons have less to do with the severity of the punishment than with what happens immediately after it ends.

The first reason is that release removes structure without replacing it. A young person leaves custody frequently with no accommodation arranged, no employment, and a criminal record that makes obtaining either substantially harder. The people most readily available to them are the ones they knew before, which is to say the ones associated with the offending in the first place. Reoffending in these circumstances is less a decision than a default.

A second reason is that custody itself interrupts the things that ordinarily hold a young life together. Education stops, apprenticeships are lost, family relationships are strained by distance and expense. Someone who enters custody at seventeen with a partial qualification frequently leaves at nineteen with none, and two years further behind peers who were already ahead.

The measures most likely to help therefore concern the transition. Arranging housing and a training placement before release, rather than after, removes the vacuum in which reoffending occurs, and supervision by a consistent individual rather than a rotating series of officials gives a young person someone to contact before a situation becomes a crime. Restricting how long a minor offence stays disclosable would also help, since a record that permanently blocks employment guarantees the outcome it was meant to prevent.
title: Why young offenders return to crime
